idiom_name: Rails ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore - the default session store, encrypted and signed cookie
implementation_notes: Rails makes this pattern the default: config.session_store :cookie_store keeps the entire session hash in one cookie, encrypted with secret_key_base through ActiveSupport::MessageEncryptor and signed, so the client can neither read nor alter it - the CookieStore documentation notes that sessions typically hold at most a user id and a flash message, both fitting the 4096-byte limit. Configure key, secure, httponly, same_site and expire_after in the session store initializer, and remember that changing secret_key_base invalidates every existing session: that is the global logout switch, because a client-held session cannot be revoked individually. Switch to a server-side store (cache, redis, active_record) when the session outgrows the cookie or must be revocable.
code_sketch:
Rails.application.config.session_store :cookie_store,
  key: "_myapp_session", secure: true, httponly: true,
  same_site: :lax, expire_after: 30.minutes

class CartController < ApplicationController
  def add
    session[:cart] = (session[:cart] || []) << params[:sku]  # back into the encrypted cookie
    redirect_to cart_path                                        # changes apply to the next request
  end
end
pitfalls: ActionDispatch::Cookies::CookieOverflow is raised the moment the session exceeds 4096 bytes; prune the session or move to a server-side store instead of chunking cookies.
secret_key_base is both the security and the continuity story: leaking it means forgeable sessions, changing it means every live session dies.
Session writes made during a request are only visible to the next request, so reading session[:cart] again in the same action still returns the old value - pair writes with a redirect.
Encrypted cookies are still client-held state: there is no per-session revocation, and a stolen cookie remains valid until it expires.
